lead: Usability evaluation checks whether a 3D interface is learnable, efficient and comfortable. It asks real users to do real tasks and records what happens. The aim is not to prove a design is good but to find where it fails before release. VR menus, AR assembly guides, surgery simulators and training applications all use it. A design can look impressive and still be slow, confusing or tiring. Evaluation turns opinion into evidence: task success, time, errors and comfort. This chapter covers guidelines, methods and metrics, and ends with a small comparison of two menu designs.
prereq: You need: selection and manipulation, travel, system control, and human factors, plus basic averages.

blocks.text: A usability guideline is a design rule that protects the user from a known failure. In 3D it must cover the body as well as the screen. The six rules below are a practical checklist.

items: Visibility: the user can see what can be done. Menus sit in a readable place, targets are large enough, and current state is visible. In a VR menu, keep the selected item highlighted and within the field of view.

Feedback: every action gives a reply. A grabbed object follows the hand, a button changes colour, and a failed selection gives a short sound or vibration. Delay above about 100 ms starts to feel disconnected.
Consistency: the same gesture means the same thing. If the trigger grabs in one scene, it should not teleport in the next. Use the same menu layout across tasks.
Error prevention: make slips hard. Use snapping, confirm delete, and avoid tiny targets at arm's length. A wrong command should be easy to undo.
User control: the user can stop, undo or change mode. Do not trap the user in an animation. Provide a clear exit from every menu.
Fatigue: design for short, supported actions. Avoid long arm raises, repeated pinch gestures and heavy head movement. Place controls in a comfortable zone.

blocks.text: These guidelines are cheap to check in a review. They do not replace a user test, but they catch many faults before users arrive.

Formative evaluation happens while the design is still changing. The aim is to find problems and fix them. It uses few users, rough prototypes and close observation. Summative evaluation happens when the design is stable. The aim is to measure performance and compare options. It uses more users, a fixed task and agreed metrics.

items: Expert review: a trained reviewer checks the interface against the guidelines and lists likely problems. It is fast and cheap, but it predicts user problems; it does not measure them.

Think-aloud: the user speaks while doing the task. The tester notes confusion, silence and workarounds. It is strong for formative work. It can slow the user, so do not use its timings as final performance data.
Task-based test: each user gets the same task, such as 'place the red block in the tray'. The tester records success, errors, time and comments. This is the backbone of summative evaluation.

blocks.text: An A/B comparison is a task-based test with two designs. Half the users see A first, half see B first. This counterbalancing reduces learning effects. The same task, instructions and scene must be used for both. A difference in completion or errors then points to the design, not to the order. Some syllabi call this whole activity evaluation of 3D user interfaces.
A metric is a number that answers one question. Choose metrics before the test, not after. The common set is:
completion rate = users who complete ÷ users who start × 100%
blocks.where: users who complete is the count of people who finish the task; users who start is the count who began it.
errors is the count of wrong actions; attempts is the count of task attempts, so one user can add more than one attempt.

items: Task time: seconds from start to success. Report median when a few users are very slow.
SUS (System Usability Scale): a 10-item questionnaire scored 0 to 100. It is a usability score, not a percentage of users. A higher score is better.
NASA-TLX (Task Load Index): a workload questionnaire with mental, physical and time demands. It is useful when two designs are equally fast but one feels harder.
Presence: a questionnaire score for the feeling of being inside the virtual world. It matters for training and entertainment, but it does not replace task success.

blocks.text: Report the denominator with every rate. '80% completion' means 16 of 20 users. '15% error rate' means 6 errors in 40 attempts. These two rates use different units: users and attempts.

sections.h3: Reading a comparison without fooling yourself

blocks.text: A/B results are only useful if the test is fair. Use the same task, same starting state and same time limit. Counterbalance the order. Keep the instructions neutral. Do not help one group more than the other. Record every attempt, including failed ones.

Look at the pattern, not one number. Design B in the figure has higher completion and lower error rate. That is a consistent win. A design with faster time but more errors may still be worse for a medical or industrial task. A design with equal success but higher NASA-TLX may tire users sooner.

Small tests are common in formative work. A result from 5 users can reveal major faults but cannot prove a small difference. For a summative claim, use enough users and report the count. Do not turn a 2-user difference into a general law.

figure.caption: Design B wins on both measures: 90% completion against 80%, and 7.5% errors against 15%. Completion is out of 20 users and errors out of 40 attempts, so each rate keeps its own denominator.

examples.question: Two VR menu designs are tested by 20 users each. The test records 40 attempts per design. Design A: 16 users complete the task; its 40 attempts contain 6 errors. Design B: 18 users complete; its 40 attempts contain 3 errors. Compute completion rate and error rate for each design. Compare them.
steps: For design A, completion rate = users who complete ÷ users who start × 100% = 16 ÷ 20 × 100% = 0.80 × 100% = 80.0%.
For design A, error rate = errors ÷ attempts × 100% = 6 ÷ 40 × 100% = 0.15 × 100% = 15.0%.
Compare: B has 10.0 percentage points more completion and 7.5 percentage points fewer errors. Both metrics favour B.
examples.answer: Design A: completion 80.0%, error 15.0%; design B: completion 90.0%, error 7.5%, so B performs better on both metrics.

traps: Completion rate uses users as the denominator. Error rate uses attempts. Mixing them gives a number that is neither.
A user who completes after many errors is still a completion. Report errors separately; do not subtract them from completions.
SUS is a 0–100 score, not a percentage of users. A SUS of 68 does not mean 68% success.
Think-aloud slows users. Do not compare task times from a think-aloud test with times from a silent test.
Presence and preference are not performance. A design can feel immersive and still be slow or error-prone.

quiz.q: What is the difference between formative and summative evaluation?
quiz.a: Formative evaluation runs during design to find and fix problems. Summative evaluation runs on a stable design to measure performance and compare options.

quiz.q: Why does error rate use attempts as the denominator rather than users?
quiz.a: Because one user can make many attempts and several errors. Attempts count opportunities for error; users count people. Using users hides repeated mistakes and can give a rate above 100%.

quiz.q: A test has 25 users. 20 complete the task. The test records 50 attempts with 5 errors. Compute completion rate and error rate.
Design A: 17 of 20 users complete; 6 errors in 50 attempts. Design B: 18 of 20 complete; 9 errors in 50 attempts. Which is better?
quiz.a: A: 85% completion, 12% error. B: 90% completion, 18% error. B completes more users but has 50% more errors. For a high-risk task, A may be safer; for a low-risk task, B may be acceptable. The decision depends on the cost of an error.

quiz.q: Name two guidelines and the failure each prevents.
quiz.a: Feedback prevents the user not knowing whether an action worked. Fatigue prevention stops long arm raises or repeated gestures from exhausting the user.

quiz.q: Why should think-aloud timings not be used as final performance data?
quiz.a: Speaking while working adds mental load and slows the task. The timing then measures the talking as well as the interface. Use think-aloud to find problems, and measure time in a silent task test.

quiz.q: Two designs have equal completion and equal task time. Design B has a higher NASA-TLX score. What does this suggest?
quiz.a: B feels harder in mental, physical or time demand. Equal speed does not mean equal comfort. B may cause more fatigue or errors in longer sessions, so investigate the load before choosing it.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, VR teams log task events and frame times, then combine these with short questionnaires after each session. Research adds eye tracking, hand-motion logs and physiological sensors to see where users hesitate or tire. Longitudinal studies ask whether gains last after a week of training. Search for '3D user interface evaluation', 'VR usability metrics', and 'NASA-TLX in VR' to go deeper.
